/-!
# Cluster primes

A cluster prime is a prime $p$ such that every even positive integer $k \le p - 3$ can be
written as the difference of two primes not exceeding $p$. By convention, $2$ is not a cluster
prime. The first $23$ odd primes (up to $89$) are all cluster primes; the first odd prime that
is not a cluster prime is $97$. Blecksmith, Erdős and Selfridge proved that the cluster primes
form a small set (the sum of their reciprocals converges), but it is not known whether there are
infinitely many of them.

The same question is Erdős Problem 17, see `FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«17»`. The
definition below follows the Wikipedia convention that $2$ is not a cluster prime.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, Cluster prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cluster_prime)
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [OEIS A038134](https://oeis.org/A038134)
* R. Blecksmith, P. Erdős, J. L. Selfridge, *Cluster primes*,
  Amer. Math. Monthly 106 (1999), 43–48. [doi:10.2307/2589585](https://doi.org/10.2307/2589585)
-/

blocks.docstring:
A prime $p$ is a *cluster prime* if every even positive integer $k \le p - 3$ can be
written as the difference $q_1 - q_2$ of two primes $q_1, q_2 \le p$. By convention, $2$ is
not a cluster prime (it would otherwise satisfy the condition vacuously).

justification.closest_existing_considered: Erdos17.IsClusterPrime (FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/17.lean); also Nat.Prime / Set.Infinite from Mathlib for the surrounding statement.
justification.name: ClusterPrime.IsClusterPrime
justification.why_needed: Mathlib has no notion of cluster prime. The repository has `Erdos17.IsClusterPrime` (FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/17.lean), but (a) it lives in a problem file, which problem files should not import, (b) it does NOT exclude p = 2 (for p = 2 the bound n ≤ −1 is vacuous so 2 is a cluster prime there), contradicting the Wikipedia convention that the decomposition table asks to respect, and (c) it quantifies over all even n including 0 rather than 'even positive'. The new definition follows the Wikipedia wording literally: `p.Prime ∧ p ≠ 2 ∧ ∀ k, Even k → 0 < k → k ≤ p - 3 → ∃ q₁ q₂, q₁.Prime ∧ q₂.Prime ∧ q₁ ≤ p ∧ q₂ ≤ p ∧ q₁ - q₂ = k`.

blocks.name: IsClusterPrime
blocks.text:
/-- A prime $p$ is a *cluster prime* if every even positive integer $k \le p - 3$ can be
written as the difference $q_1 - q_2$ of two primes $q_1, q_2 \le p$. By convention, $2$ is
not a cluster prime (it would otherwise satisfy the condition vacuously). -/
def IsClusterPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ p ≠ 2 ∧
    ∀ k : ℕ, Even k → 0 < k → k ≤ p - 3 →
      ∃ q₁ q₂ : ℕ, q₁.Prime ∧ q₂.Prime ∧
        q₁ ≤ p ∧ q₂ ≤ p ∧ q₁ - q₂ = k

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no question (Prop: the set of cluster primes is infinite, stated as `answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Infinite ...`); a cluster prime is a prime p such that every even positive k ≤ p − 3 is a difference of two primes ≤ p, and by convention p = 2 is excluded (it would otherwise qualify vacuously), which does not affect infinitude but should be respected in the definition.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same faithful proposition (answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Infinite of the cluster primes, with a bespoke predicate: prime, p ≠ 2 by convention, every even positive k ≤ p − 3 is a difference of two primes ≤ p). All compile with only the sorry warning; the ℕ-vs-ℤ subtraction variants are equivalent under the constraints (p ≥ 3 makes p − 3 exact; 0 < k makes truncated q₁ − q₂ = k harmless). c07 chosen as the base: clean ℕ definition, thorough module docstring with all sources, and compiled API tests pinning the boundary behaviour (2 excluded, 3 and 5 and 23 included, 97 excluded) as CONTRIBUTING requests for bespoke definitions. Edits: added c08's cross-reference to the existing Erdos17 formalization (which differs only in admitting 2) to the module docstring, and rewrapped two lines over 100 characters.

context: In number theory, a cluster prime is a prime number p such that every even positive integer k ≤ p − 3 can be written as the difference between two prime numbers not exceeding p (OEIS: A038134). For example, the number 23 is a cluster prime because 23 − 3 = 20, and every even integer from 2 to 20, inclusive, is the difference of at least one pair of prime numbers not exceeding 23:

decomposition_objections.text: None. One remark for reviewers: the repository's existing `Erdos17.IsClusterPrime` (ErdosProblems/17.lean) formalizes the same notion without the p ≠ 2 exclusion and with k = 0 allowed; the two definitions agree on all odd primes, so `erdos_17` and `ClusterPrime.cluster_prime` are equivalent statements, but the new file follows the Wikipedia convention as the table instructs.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Cluster primes

A cluster prime is a prime $p$ such that every even positive integer $k \le p - 3$ can be
written as the difference of two primes not exceeding $p$. By convention, $2$ is not a cluster
prime. The first $23$ odd primes (up to $89$) are all cluster primes; the first odd prime that
is not a cluster prime is $97$. Blecksmith, Erdős and Selfridge proved that the cluster primes
form a small set (the sum of their reciprocals converges), but it is not known whether there are
infinitely many of them.

The same question is Erdős Problem 17, see `FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«17»`. The
definition below follows the Wikipedia convention that $2$ is not a cluster prime.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, Cluster prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cluster_prime)
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [OEIS A038134](https://oeis.org/A038134)
* R. Blecksmith, P. Erdős, J. L. Selfridge, *Cluster primes*,
  Amer. Math. Monthly 106 (1999), 43–48. [doi:10.2307/2589585](https://doi.org/10.2307/2589585)
-/

namespace ClusterPrime

/-- A prime $p$ is a *cluster prime* if every even positive integer $k \le p - 3$ can be
written as the difference $q_1 - q_2$ of two primes $q_1, q_2 \le p$. By convention, $2$ is
not a cluster prime (it would otherwise satisfy the condition vacuously). -/
def IsClusterPrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ p ≠ 2 ∧
    ∀ k : ℕ, Even k → 0 < k → k ≤ p - 3 →
      ∃ q₁ q₂ : ℕ, q₁.Prime ∧ q₂.Prime ∧
        q₁ ≤ p ∧ q₂ ≤ p ∧ q₁ - q₂ = k

/-- Are there infinitely many cluster primes, i.e. primes $p \ne 2$ such that every even
positive integer $k \le p - 3$ is the difference of two primes not exceeding $p$? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem cluster_prime : answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | IsClusterPrime p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- By convention, $2$ is not a cluster prime. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isClusterPrime_two : ¬ IsClusterPrime 2 := by
  simp [IsClusterPrime]

/-- The prime $3$ is a cluster prime: there is no even positive integer $k \le 3 - 3 = 0$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isClusterPrime_three : IsClusterPrime 3 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, fun k _ hk0 hk3 => ?_⟩
  omega

/-- The prime $5$ is a cluster prime: $2 = 5 - 3$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isClusterPrime_five : IsClusterPrime 5 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, fun k hk hk0 hk3 => ?_⟩
  obtain rfl : k = 2 := by rw [Nat.even_iff] at hk; omega
  exact ⟨5, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, le_rfl, by norm_num, rfl⟩

/-- The prime $23$ is a cluster prime, as in the Wikipedia article: every even integer from
$2$ to $20$ is the difference of two primes not exceeding $23$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isClusterPrime_23 : IsClusterPrime 23 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, fun k hk hk0 hk3 => ?_⟩
  interval_cases k
  all_goals first
    | exact absurd hk (by decide)
    | exact ⟨5, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨7, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨11, 5, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨11, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨13, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨17, 5, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨17, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨19, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨23, 5, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩
    | exact ⟨23, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, rfl⟩

/-- The prime $97$ is not a cluster prime: $88 \le 94$ is not the difference of two primes
not exceeding $97$. It is the smallest odd prime that is not a cluster prime. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isClusterPrime_97 : ¬ IsClusterPrime 97 := by
  rintro ⟨-, -, h⟩
  obtain ⟨q₁, q₂, hq₁, hq₂, hq₁p, -, hd⟩ :=
    h 88 (by decide) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
  obtain rfl : q₁ = q₂ + 88 := by omega
  have : q₂ ≤ 9 := by omega
  interval_cases q₂ <;> revert hq₁ hq₂ <;> norm_num

end ClusterPrime

items: The terse list entry 'Are there infinitely many cluster primes?' is formalized as `answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | IsClusterPrime p}`, so answer(True) = infinitely many, answer(False) = finitely many; the definition of cluster prime is taken from the Wikipedia article 'Cluster prime'.

Convention '2 is not considered to be a cluster prime' is encoded as the conjunct `p ≠ 2` inside the definition (as the decomposition table requests). It does not affect the infinitude question but makes the predicate match Wikipedia/OEIS A038134 exactly.

'Every even positive integer k ≤ p − 3' is encoded as `Even k → 0 < k → k ≤ p - 3`. Since p is prime and ≠ 2, p ≥ 3, so the natural-number subtraction `p - 3` is exact (no truncation). Consequently 3 is vacuously a cluster prime, matching OEIS A038134 (3, 5, 7, ...) and the article's 'first 23 odd primes (up to 89) are all cluster primes'.

'k is the difference between two primes not exceeding p' is encoded as `∃ q₁ q₂, q₁.Prime ∧ q₂.Prime ∧ q₁ ≤ p ∧ q₂ ≤ p ∧ q₁ - q₂ = k` in ℕ. Because 0 < k, `q₁ - q₂ = k` forces q₂ < q₁, so the truncated subtraction coincides with the integer difference; 'not exceeding' is the non-strict bound ≤ p.

Tests included as sanity checks of the definition: ¬IsClusterPrime 2 (convention), IsClusterPrime 3 (smallest/vacuous case), IsClusterPrime 5, IsClusterPrime 23 (the article's worked example), ¬IsClusterPrime 97 (the article's first odd non-cluster prime, via 88 = 97 − 9 not being a difference of primes ≤ 97).
Module docstring references include https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/cluster_prime (as required), the Wikipedia list page, OEIS A038134, and Blecksmith–Erdős–Selfridge (1999).

reviewer_notes: The source entry is terse; the definition of cluster prime is taken from the linked Wikipedia article (agreeing with OEIS A038134 and Blecksmith–Erdős–Selfridge 1999). No candidate omitted the slot and no omission reasons needed weighing. Reviewer note: the repository already contains Erdos17.IsClusterPrime / erdos_17 (ErdosProblems/17.lean) for the same question; that definition counts 2 as a (vacuous) cluster prime and allows k = 0, so it differs from the Wikipedia convention by exactly the element 2. The two infinitude statements are therefore equivalent, but the decomposition table asked for the Wikipedia convention to be respected, so a bespoke ClusterPrime.IsClusterPrime with p ≠ 2 is used and the module docstring points to the Erdős 17 file. Boundary check: 3 is vacuously a cluster prime (no even positive k ≤ 0), matching OEIS A038134 which begins 3, 5, 7, …. Final file compiled with `lake env lean --json`: only warning is `declaration uses 'sorry'` on the research-open theorem.
